intro: Every tree on this page stands outside Potsdam itself, across the Glienicke bridge in Berlin or further still. Four are protected there by the Land of Berlin, a twelve-minute tram ride from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof: two small-leaved limes, one named the King's Linden in the register itself, and two oaks, the further nearly six metres round. Two more stand further out on Pfaueninsel, a former royal pleasure island reached only by ferry, one of them an oak with a door built into its trunk.
meta_description: Six protected trees near Potsdam, across the Glienicke bridge and beyond: the King's Linden, a 300-year oak, and an oak with a door cut into it.
question_meta: The oldest tree by the Glienicke bridge is the Jagerhof oak, roughly 300 years old and 566cm round in 2023. Where it stands, and what else is there.
question_answer: The oldest tree on this page is the oak at the Jägerhof in Volkspark Klein-Glienicke, roughly 300 years old and 566 centimetres round when it was last measured in 2023. Roughly, because no register here records ages at all: Berlin's list of natural monuments, which protects all four of these trees, gives each one a number, a species, a cadastral parcel and a sentence saying where it stands, and stops. The 300-year figure comes from a German veteran-tree archive reasoning backwards from the Jägerhof itself, which was built before 1830 with the oak already standing beside it and, in that archive's judgement, already more than a century old. The other three trees, two small-leaved limes and a second oak, have no published age anywhere, so this page gives them none rather than a guess.
question_context: Four of these six trees sit in a strip of parkland that reads as Potsdam and is administered as Berlin. The Glienicke bridge is the border, the tram from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof crosses it in twelve minutes, and the parks on the eastern bank form part of the UNESCO World Heritage site covering the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin. Those four are protected as natural monuments by the Land of Berlin, a legal designation rather than a survey: the register records neither age nor girth nor condition, so three of them carry no measurements here. The exception is the Jägerhof oak, taped at 566 centimetres in 2023 by a German veteran-tree archive, the best documented and by a distance the largest of the four. Three stand within a few hundred metres of the bridge; the oak is fifteen to twenty minutes further south. The other two, both sessile oaks, stand well beyond this cluster on Pfaueninsel and need their own ferry trip, described separately rather than folded into the same walk. Three planes in the walled garden behind the hunting lodge are left off, because nobody could confirm public access.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree near Potsdam?
faq.a: The oak at the Jägerhof in Volkspark Klein-Glienicke, roughly 300 years old. The estimate comes from a German veteran-tree archive, which measured it at 566 centimetres round in 2023 and reasoned back from the Jägerhof, built before 1830 with the oak already standing. Berlin's natural-monument register carries no age field, so nothing here is a dated planting record.

faq.q: Are these trees actually in Potsdam?
faq.a: No, and the page says so on purpose. Four stand on the Berlin bank of the Havel, in Berlin-Wannsee, immediately across the Glienicke bridge from Potsdam; two more stand further out still, on Pfaueninsel. In practice the first four are a Potsdam walk: tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof reaches the bridge in about twelve minutes.

Yes. All six stand in open public parkland or nature reserve with no ticket for the trees themselves (Pfaueninsel charges a small entry fee to the island and its ferry), and the whole area is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin.

faq.q: Can I see all four in one walk?
faq.a: The first four, yes, and it is a good one. The two limes and the first oak are within a few hundred metres of the bridge; the Jägerhof oak is a further fifteen to twenty minutes south along the park path above the Havel, near the Krughorn headland. Allow about two hours for the round trip with stops.

faq.q: What about the two Pfaueninsel oaks?
faq.a: They stand on a separate island further out, not part of the Glienicke walk. Reaching them needs a bus change and a short paid ferry crossing, roughly 35 to 45 minutes each way from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof, so treat them as their own trip. Once there, the Door Oak and the Schlosswiese Oak stand about a hundred metres apart.

trees.name: The Linden of Park Jagdschloss Glienicke

location.address: Park Jagdschloss Glienicke, northwestern section, about 200m southeast of Glienicker Brücke, Königstraße, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf), on the Potsdam border
location.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge

trees.story: Two hundred metres from this lime tree is the bridge where the Cold War traded people. Glienicker Brücke carried the spy exchanges between the Americans and the Soviets, and the border ran down the middle of the water beneath it. The tree stands on the eastern bank, which is to say in Berlin, though it is a twelve-minute tram ride from Potsdam's main station and a long way from anything a Berliner thinks of as the city. It is a small-leaved lime, a Winter-Linde, protected by the Land of Berlin as a natural monument under the number 6-99/B, standing in the open parkland of Park Jagdschloss Glienicke around the old hunting lodge. What that protection does not come with is information. The register gives a species, a parcel number and a place, and records no age, no girth and no note on the tree's condition, because it is a legal instrument rather than a survey. So this entry is thinner than most here, and it says so. One official source names the tree and nothing else we could find does. What that source does establish is the thing worth walking for: somebody looked at this particular lime, among all the trees in a large park, and decided it was not to be cut down.
trees.how_to_recognise: In the open parkland around the hunting lodge, not in the walled garden behind the building. The second protected lime is 200 metres east, on Königstraße opposite the Wiesenteich pond.
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round. Stands in Park Jagdschloss Glienicke, the open parkland around the hunting lodge, not the fenced institute garden behind the building itself
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a short walk into the park
trees.notes: Land Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-99/B (Tilia cordata, Winter-Linde), Flur 110037-14-82, matching the official gazette PDF word for word. Flagged: only one source found, the Land Berlin register itself, and no independent second source. The register carries no age or vitality field, which is standard for this dataset.

trees.name: The King's Linden

location.address: Schlossgarten Glienicke, on Königstraße opposite the Wiesenteich pond, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf), on the Potsdam border
location.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge

trees.story: People took tea under this lime, and the floor they did it on is still there. A mosaic pavement near the Lions Fountain in the Schlossgarten marks the spot where visitors to Prince Carl of Prussia's estate sat beneath the tree, and the park's own account calls it one of the most impressive solitary trees on the estate. Berlin's register of natural monuments agrees in its own dry way. It gives the tree a number, 6-100/B, and a name, Königslinde, the King's Linden, which is unusual in a document that mostly records species and parcel numbers and then stops. The garden around it was laid out from 1816 by Peter Joseph Lenné for Prince Carl, an English landscape of long sightlines on a Prussian riverbank, and it is now part of the UNESCO World Heritage site covering the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin. It is open, free, and has no gate. Neither the register nor the park's history gives this lime an age or a girth, so it gets neither here. It stands on Königstraße opposite the Wiesenteich pond, on the Berlin side of the Glienicke bridge, twelve minutes from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof on the 93 tram, and it is the tree on this walk that people actually sat under.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the lime blossom opens and the scent carries across the lawn

trees.how_to_recognise: The big solitary lime on the Königstraße side of the Schlossgarten, opposite the Wiesenteich, with the mosaic floor near the Lions Fountain. The other protected lime is 200 metres west, by the hunting lodge.
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round, no gate, no hours and no admission. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a short walk into the Schlossgarten
trees.notes: Land Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-100/B, named Konigslinde in the register itself, Flur 110037-14-85. Second source is English Wikipedia's Park Glienicke article (the solitary-tree description and the tea-party mosaic). Flagged because neither source is a recent dated photograph or observation; the register was pulled from a live Land Berlin geodata service on 2026-08-07. No age or girth in either source.

trees.name: The Schlosspark Glienicke Oak

location.address: Schlosspark Glienicke, about 150m north of Königstraße 35C, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf), on the Potsdam border
location.neighbourhood: Schlosspark Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge

trees.story: Berlin protects this oak by law and almost nothing else about it is on record. It appears in the Land of Berlin's register of natural monuments as 6-105/B, a Stiel-Eiche, a Pedunculate Oak, standing about 150 metres north of Königstraße 35C in Schlosspark Glienicke. That entry gives a species, a parcel and a position, and there it ends: no age, no girth, no word on the tree's condition, because the register exists to say what may not be felled rather than to describe what is there. So this is a tree you go and read for yourself. It grows in the landscape garden Peter Joseph Lenné began laying out in 1816 for Prince Carl of Prussia, a park of engineered views designed to look accidental, now inside the UNESCO World Heritage site that covers the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin. Oaks are the long-lived furniture of gardens like this one, and often older than the design around them. The one fact the register does carry says something a tape measure would not: out of the thousands of trees standing in this parkland, somebody walked up to this one and wrote it down. It is a few minutes further into the park than the two protected limes. If you get a tape round it, we would like the number.
trees.access: Free, open to the public year-round, the same parkland as the two limes, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the palaces and parks of Potsdam and Berlin
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then a walk of a few minutes further into the park than the lime trees
trees.notes: Land Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-105/B (Quercus robur, Stiel-Eiche), Flur 110037-14-130, matching the imported WFS register entry and the official gazette word for word. Flagged: one source only, no independent second source, and no genuine girth or age figure found. A search summary claiming a '130cm circumference' was checked against the source PDF and is the Flur parcel number, not a measurement; it is deliberately not recorded here and must not be reintroduced.

trees.name: The Jägerhof Oak

location.address: Volkspark Klein-Glienicke, at the Jägerhof, south of the Krughorn headland, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf), on the Potsdam border
location.neighbourhood: Volkspark Klein-Glienicke, Berlin side of the Glienicke Bridge

trees.story: The oak was here first. The Jägerhof in Volkspark Klein-Glienicke went up some time before 1830, and by the reckoning of the German veteran-tree archive that measured this tree, it was already more than a hundred years old when the builders arrived. That puts its beginning before roughly 1730, which makes 300 years a fair estimate and not a precise one. Nobody has cored it, and Berlin's register of natural monuments, which protects it as 6-73/B, has no age field to put a figure in. The girth is firmer: 566 centimetres at chest height, taped in 2023. Nearly six metres of trunk, and by a wide margin the heaviest tree on this walk. It stands high above the Havel path near the Krughorn headland, south along the park from the Glienicke bridge and about fifteen to twenty minutes on foot from the other three trees here. Berlin bought the estate in the 1930s and opened it to the public, so the ground under this oak has been walkable for the better part of a century. Before that it was hunting country, which is what a Jägerhof is for. The lodge was built for the sport. The oak was simply standing in the way of it, and outlived the whole arrangement.

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are down and the whole frame of the old crown shows

trees.access: Free, open to the public. Volkspark Klein-Glienicke was opened to the public in the 1930s when Berlin acquired the estate; the Jägerhof and the ground around it are publicly accessible, high above the Havel-side path near the Krughorn
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to the Glienicker Brücke stop, about 12 minutes, then roughly a 15-20 minute walk south along the park path to the Jägerhof
trees.notes: Land Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-73/B (Quercus robur, Stiel-Eiche). Second, independent source: Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv, a German veteran-tree archive unaffiliated with the Berlin government, giving 566cm girth measured 2023 at 1.3m and a photo dated 2011. The age follows that archive's own reasoning (Jagerhof built before 1830, oak likely already over 100 years old then), so 250-350 is a source-grounded range rather than an invented figure. The strongest-evidenced of the four.

trees.name: The Door Oak of Pfaueninsel

location.address: Pfaueninsel, about 100m northeast of the ferry landing (Faehranleger), reached by the short Havel ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf)

trees.story:
A door was cut into this oak, and the tree kept growing around it. Somewhere in the nineteenth century, on a Prussian royal family's private pleasure island, someone shaped an opening straight through the trunk of a sessile oak and left it there. Peacocks still roam the island it stands on, which is what gives Pfaueninsel its name, and the folly fits the place: nothing here was meant to look ordinary.

Berlin's register of natural monuments lists it simply as a Trauben-Eiche, a sessile oak, designated in 1993, with none of the theatre attached. A German veteran-tree archive fills the rest in: 5.58 metres round the trunk, an age estimate of roughly 250 years, and a visit dated May 2025 recording it alive and in good condition, the most recent confirmation found.

It stands well past the Glienicke walk this page otherwise covers. Reaching it means a bus change and a short paid ferry crossing, more like thirty five to forty five minutes each way from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof than the twelve-minute tram to the other four trees here. It earns the detour anyway: an oak with a door in it, on an island built for peacocks and a king's fancy, is not a thing you see twice.
trees.access: Free entry to the Pfaueninsel nature reserve; the island itself is reached only by a short ferry crossing from Nikolskoer Weg (a few minutes, small return fare; published ferry hours are daily 10:00-18:00, March to October)
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to Glienicker Brucke (about 12 min), then bus 316 towards Wannsee to the Nikolskoer Weg stop (about 5 min), then the Pfaueninsel ferry (2-3 min crossing). Allow roughly 35-45 minutes door to door, further than the other four trees on this page
trees.notes: Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-101/B (Trauben-Eiche / Quercus petraea), designated 1993-03-02. Independently identified via baumkunde.de entry #6402, within about 15m of the register point: a door-shaped opening cut into the trunk, visible in photos from 2005 onward, recorded vital at a visit dated 25.05.2025. Girth 5.58m, dated only 01.01.2017 (likely a placeholder date on the source). Age ~250 years is baumkunde's own estimate. Species conflict note: baumkunde's own auto-translated English page mislabels this Pedunculate Oak, but both the German common name (Trauben-Eiche) and the register's Latin binomial agree on Quercus petraea (Sessile Oak); trusted petraea. Genuinely further from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof than pot_001-004, shipped as an honest further excursion rather than folded into the same walk, per the day-trip precedent (Blarney/Fota for Cork, Coole Park for Galway).

trees.name: The Schlosswiese Oak of Pfaueninsel

location.address: Pfaueninsel, on the Schlosswiese meadow about 100m northeast of Schloss Pfaueninsel, reached by the short Havel ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, Berlin-Wannsee (Steglitz-Zehlendorf)

trees.story:
A hundred metres from the Door Oak, on the meadow below Schloss Pfaueninsel, stands a second registered sessile oak with a trick of its own. About two and a half metres up, its trunk splits into five curved stems rather than one, a shape a pruning around 2015 seems to have encouraged rather than damaged: German tree archivists who have visited it repeatedly since 2002 recorded vigorous regrowth afterward, and the most recent visit, in May 2025, still found it vital.

Two independent measurements put its girth around 5.6 metres, taken six years apart and close enough to agree on a tree still slowly thickening. Its age is put at roughly 200 years, a touch younger than its door-cut neighbour nearby. Both carry the same official protection, Berlin's 1993 register of natural monuments, in a paragraph that names a species and a spot and says nothing about what makes either worth the walk.

Reaching the meadow means the same detour as the Door Oak: a tram, a bus, and a short paid ferry from Nikolskoer Weg, roughly 35 to 45 minutes each way from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof. Pfaueninsel was built as a private fantasy for a Prussian king, all follies and imported animals, and these two oaks are what is left standing from the working parkland around it.
trees.access: Free entry to the Pfaueninsel nature reserve; the island itself is reached only by a short ferry crossing from Nikolskoer Weg (a few minutes, small return fare; published hours are daily 10:00-18:00, March to October)
trees.transport: Tram 93 from Potsdam Hauptbahnhof to Glienicker Brucke (about 12 min), then bus 316 towards Wannsee to the Nikolskoer Weg stop (about 5 min), then the Pfaueninsel ferry (2-3 min crossing). Allow roughly 35-45 minutes door to door, further than the other four trees on this page
trees.notes: Berlin Naturdenkmal register id 6-102/B (Trauben-Eiche / Quercus petraea), designated 1993-03-02. Three sources agreeing within metres: baumkunde.de #2135 (girth 5.58m measured 19.02.2025, height 16.0m, vital 25.05.2025, vigorous regrowth after a c.2015 pruning) and Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv (565cm measured 2019, trunk dividing at about 2.5m into one main stem plus five curved secondary stems, documented visits 2002-2019). Girth conflict (5.58m vs 5.65m) plausibly explained by six years of growth, both figures kept rather than one discarded. Species conflict: Ostdeutsches Baumarchiv's own species field says Quercus robur despite titling the tree Traubeneiche; register and baumkunde agree on Quercus petraea, trusted here. Best-evidenced of the two Pfaueninsel candidates. Same access/distance caveat as pot_005.
